system:
You are the analysis agent of a reporting platform for Australia's threatened species. Conservation practitioners — people in government agencies, NGOs and recovery teams who decide where to survey, what to protect and what to escalate — read what you produce. You have read-only SQL access to the platform's database and produce insights from it, each grounded in queries you ran.

# The data

PostgreSQL 17 with PostGIS 3.5. The corpus is every occurrence record the Atlas of Living Australia (ALA) tags as nationally threatened (EPBC Critically Endangered, Endangered or Vulnerable), observed January 2015 to 2026-09-30, from one bulk download (DOI 10.26197/ala.40eee344-07ce-48d2-9ec2-be39574ff4c7): about 2.1 million records, 1,850 taxa, 300+ contributing datasets. Alongside it are all-taxa effort counts per 0.1° cell per month for the same period.

corpus.analysable_occurrences — VIEW — the records to analyse: occurrences that are valid, dated, and not from telemetry (animal-tracking) datasets. Includes population ('wild' or 'managed' — managed means a fenced haven, reintroduction or other managed population, set from the dataset or from corpus.managed_populations) and dataset_kind (the dataset's own kind). Prefer this over occurrences.
  columns: record_id text, source text, source_record_id text, occurrence_id text, harvest_id text, snapshot_page text, fetched_at timestamp with time zone, data_resource_uid text, license text, taxon_concept_id text, scientific_name text, vernacular_name text, national_status text, event_date timestamp with time zone, first_loaded_at timestamp with time zone, decimal_latitude double precision, decimal_longitude double precision, coordinate_uncertainty_m double precision, state_province text, ibra_region text, locality text, geom USER-DEFINED, basis_of_record text, individual_count integer, recorded_by_pseudonym text, source_assertions ARRAY, is_valid boolean, issue_count integer, cell_lat numeric, cell_lon numeric, event_day date, managed_by_rule boolean, dataset_kind text, population text

corpus.datasets — TABLE — contributing datasets; kind is 'wild', 'managed' (fenced havens, reintroductions) or 'telemetry' (excluded from analysable_occurrences).
  columns: data_resource_uid text, name text, kind text, kind_reason text, first_seen_at timestamp with time zone

corpus.effort_cells — TABLE — record counts (threatened or not, telemetry excluded) per 0.1° cell per month, per taxon_group: 'all' (every taxon), or 'Aves', 'Mammalia', 'Reptilia', 'Amphibia', 'Plantae' (that group only). The denominator for reporting rates. Join on cell_lat/cell_lon and month, and always filter taxon_group — summing across groups double-counts.
  columns: cell_lat numeric, cell_lon numeric, period_start date, period_end date, records integer, harvest_id text, taxon_group text

corpus.harvest_runs — TABLE — provenance of each harvest (the corpus download and the effort counts).
  columns: harvest_id text, harvest_key text, run_id text, source text, description text, query jsonb, started_at timestamp with time zone, finished_at timestamp with time zone, expected_records integer, retrieved_records integer, complete boolean, corpus_hash text, request_count integer, warnings jsonb, analysis jsonb, loaded_at timestamp with time zone

corpus.managed_populations — TABLE — curated rules marking managed populations: a taxon in a state (optionally narrowed to an IBRA region and a dataset), e.g. Bilby in NSW, where it survives only in fenced havens, or Woylie in AWC's Mt Gibson haven. Already applied in analysable_occurrences.population.
  columns: taxon_concept_id text, state_province text, note text, rule_id integer, ibra_region text, data_resource_uid text

corpus.occurrences — TABLE — every canonical occurrence record, telemetry included. event_date is the observation instant (timestamptz); event_day is its Australian Eastern local date. geom is a PostGIS Point (SRID 4326); cell_lat/cell_lon are the 0.1° grid cell (rounded to nearest, as ALA assigns them).
  columns: record_id text, source text, source_record_id text, occurrence_id text, harvest_id text, snapshot_page text, fetched_at timestamp with time zone, data_resource_uid text, license text, taxon_concept_id text, scientific_name text, vernacular_name text, national_status text, event_date timestamp with time zone, first_loaded_at timestamp with time zone, decimal_latitude double precision, decimal_longitude double precision, coordinate_uncertainty_m double precision, state_province text, ibra_region text, locality text, geom USER-DEFINED, basis_of_record text, individual_count integer, recorded_by_pseudonym text, source_assertions ARRAY, is_valid boolean, issue_count integer, cell_lat numeric, cell_lon numeric, event_day date, managed_by_rule boolean

corpus.taxa — TABLE — one row per taxon (key taxon_concept_id); national_status is the EPBC status ALA attached.
  columns: taxon_concept_id text, scientific_name text, vernacular_name text, taxon_rank text, kingdom text, phylum text, taxon_class text, taxon_order text, family text, genus text, national_status text, status_seen_at timestamp with time zone

corpus.taxon_tiers — VIEW — per taxon: analysable records since 2015, last_record_day, and statistical_tier (≥100 records since 2015).
  columns: taxon_concept_id text, scientific_name text, vernacular_name text, national_status text, records_since_2015 bigint, last_record_day date, statistical_tier boolean

Useful facts: EPSG:3577 (Australian Albers, equal-area, metres) is available for gridding and areas; ibra_region is the IBRA 7 bioregion (null offshore — IBRA covers land only); coordinate_uncertainty_m is the radius the true position may lie within.

**Dates: use event_day** (the Australian Eastern local date) for every date window, count by period and date you report — not event_date, which is an instant stored in UTC and would put early-morning Australian records on the previous day.

# Known properties of this data — read before interpreting anything

- **Records measure effort as much as animals.** These are mostly opportunistic records. All-taxa recording roughly doubled between 2017–19 and 2022–24 (about 1.9×), so counts and range measures grow with effort. Use corpus.effort_cells as a denominator where it matters.
- **Recent months are incomplete.** Datasets reach ALA months to a year late: January–August 2026 holds about 20% of the records January–August 2024 holds, and eBird (the largest dataset) has not loaded 2026 at all. A recent decline is not evidence of anything until this is accounted for.
- **Sources start and stop.** A compilation that ends in 2020, or a targeted survey wound up inside an ongoing state atlas, looks exactly like range loss. Check which datasets carry a taxon's records in each period before calling a change real.
- **Locations vary in precision.** About half the analysable records are located to within 2 km; about a third state no uncertainty; ALA generalises many sensitive species to roughly 10 km.
- **Managed populations** (population = 'managed': fenced havens, reintroductions) are in the analysable view and are not wild trend.
- **National status** is as ALA attached it. Never infer, change or second-guess a taxon's conservation status.
- Taxonomy can shift: a taxon "disappearing" from a region can be a name re-assignment.

# How to work

- Call run_sql with one SELECT (or WITH … SELECT) per call, no trailing statements. Results are capped at 200 rows and queries time out after 30 s, so aggregate in SQL rather than pulling rows. Each call returns a query_id.
- Record each insight with record_insight as soon as it is established. Every insight cites the query_ids whose results support it, and every number in it must be a value those queries returned or simple arithmetic on them. Do not state figures you did not query.
- taxon_concept_id must be copied exactly from corpus.taxa; when an insight is about several taxa, put the main one there (or null) and list the others in related_taxa; region is an IBRA region name exactly as in ibra_region, or null for a national insight; period_start and period_end are the window the insight describes.
- Say how confident you are and why, in the confidence field: record counts, the datasets involved, effort, precision, and any artefact that could explain the pattern.
- When you have recorded everything worth recording, stop.

tools.name: run_sql
tools.description: Run one read-only SQL query (a single SELECT or WITH … SELECT) against the corpus. Returns a query_id, the columns and up to 200 rows. Cite the query_id in any insight that relies on the result.

sql.description: One SELECT or WITH … SELECT statement.

purpose.description: One line: what this query is for.

tools.name: record_insight
tools.description: Record one insight. Every figure must come from the cited queries.

category.description: A short label of your own for the kind of insight.

taxon_concept_id.description: Exactly as in corpus.taxa, or null for a non-taxon insight.

related_taxa.description: Optional: other taxon_concept_ids this insight is about, exactly as in corpus.taxa.

region.description: IBRA region name exactly as in ibra_region, or null for national.

period_start.description: YYYY-MM-DD — start of the window the insight describes.

figures.description: The numbers behind the insight, as returned by your queries.

confidence.description: Why this should or should not be trusted: records, datasets, effort, precision, possible artefacts.

summary.description: One or two sentences a practitioner can act on.

query_ids.description: The run_sql query_ids whose results support this insight.

messages.content:
It is October 2026. A conservation practitioner responsible for Australia's threatened species asks: from this data, what should I know right now — what has changed, what is concerning, what is new, and where are we blind?

Investigate as you judge best and record each insight worth their attention — aim for the most important 20 to 40. For each, be explicit about confidence and about any data artefact that could explain the pattern.

input.sql: SELECT extract(year from event_day)::int yr, count(*) n, count(*) filter (where population='managed') managed, count(distinct taxon_concept_id) taxa, count(distinct data_resource_uid) ds FROM corpus.analysable_occurrences GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
input.purpose: Annual record overview

input.sql: SELECT ds.data_resource_uid, ds.name, ds.kind, ds.kind_reason, count(o.*) n, min(o.event_day), max(o.event_day) FROM corpus.datasets ds LEFT JOIN corpus.occurrences o USING (data_resource_uid) WHERE ds.kind<>'wild' GROUP BY 1,2,3,4 ORDER BY n DESC

WITH o AS (
 SELECT a.taxon_concept_id, a.cell_lat, a.cell_lon, CASE WHEN event_day between '2017-01-01' and '2019-12-31' THEN 1 ELSE 2 END p,
  CASE WHEN t.kingdom='Plantae' THEN 'Plantae' WHEN t.taxon_class IN ('Aves','Mammalia','Reptilia','Amphibia') THEN t.taxon_class ELSE 'all' END grp
 FROM corpus.analysable_occurrences a JOIN corpus.taxa t USING (taxon_concept_id)
 WHERE population='wild' AND (event_day between '2017-01-01' and '2019-12-31' OR event_day between '2022-01-01' and '2024-12-31') AND cell_lat IS NOT NULL),
tc AS (SELECT taxon_concept_id, grp, count(*) filter (where p=1) n1, count(*) filter (where p=2) n2, count(distinct cell_lat||','||cell_lon) filter (where p=1) c1, count(distinct cell_lat||','||cell_lon) filter (where p=2) c2 FROM o GROUP BY 1,2 HAVING count(*)>=200),
cells AS (SELECT DISTINCT o.taxon_concept_id, o.grp, o.cell_lat, o.cell_lon FROM o JOIN tc USING (taxon_concept_id)),
eff AS (SELECT c.taxon_concept_id, sum(e.records) filter (where e.period_start between '2017-01-01' and '2019-12-01') e1, sum(e.records) filter (where e.period_start between '2022-01-01' and '2024-12-01') e2
 FROM cells c JOIN corpus.effort_cells e ON e.cell_lat=c.cell_lat AND e.cell_lon=c.cell_lon AND e.taxon_group=c.grp GROUP BY 1)
SELECT t.vernacular_name, t.scientific_name, t.national_status, tc.grp, n1, n2, c1, c2, round((n2::numeric/nullif(e2,0))/(nullif(n1,0)::numeric/e1),2) rate_ratio, round(e2::numeric/e1,2) eff_ratio, tc.taxon_concept_id
FROM tc JOIN eff USING (taxon_concept_id) JOIN corpus.taxa t USING (taxon_concept_id)
WHERE n1>=100 AND n2>=0 ORDER BY rate_ratio ASC NULLS FIRST LIMIT 40

confidence.basis: Victorian Biodiversity Atlas counts by year and class. The fall is abrupt (2019 to 2020) and covers many bird species at once, which points to a change in what the atlas receives or shares, not in the birds. VBA's 2025–26 shortfall also reflects normal delivery lag.

input.summary: Victorian Biodiversity Atlas bird records fell about tenfold after 2019 (7,281 in 2017; 657 in 2020; 953 in 2024), and the atlas has barely delivered anything for 2025–26 (2,909 and 135 records). Unadjusted Victorian trends for Regent Honeyeater, South-eastern Red-tailed Black-cockatoo, Painted Honeyeater and Mallee Emu-wren are inflated by this source drop. Compare these birds using eBird and Birdata, which run continuously, not all sources pooled.

WITH o AS (
 SELECT a.taxon_concept_id, a.cell_lat, a.cell_lon, CASE WHEN event_day < '2020-01-01' THEN 1 ELSE 2 END p
 FROM corpus.analysable_occurrences a JOIN corpus.taxa t USING (taxon_concept_id)
 WHERE population='wild' AND t.taxon_class='Aves' AND data_resource_uid='dr2009' AND (event_day between '2017-01-01' and '2019-12-31' OR event_day between '2022-01-01' and '2024-12-31') AND cell_lat IS NOT NULL),
tc AS (SELECT taxon_concept_id, count(*) filter (where p=1) n1, count(*) filter (where p=2) n2, count(distinct cell_lat||','||cell_lon) filter (where p=1) c1, count(distinct cell_lat||','||cell_lon) filter (where p=2) c2 FROM o GROUP BY 1 HAVING count(*) filter (where p=1)>=200),
cells AS (SELECT DISTINCT o.taxon_concept_id, o.cell_lat, o.cell_lon FROM o JOIN tc USING (taxon_concept_id)),
eff AS (SELECT c.taxon_concept_id, sum(e.records) filter (where e.period_start between '2017-01-01' and '2019-12-01') e1, sum(e.records) filter (where e.period_start between '2022-01-01' and '2024-12-01') e2
 FROM cells c JOIN corpus.effort_cells e ON e.cell_lat=c.cell_lat AND e.cell_lon=c.cell_lon AND e.taxon_group='Aves' GROUP BY 1)
SELECT t.vernacular_name, n1, n2, c1, c2, round((n2::numeric/e2)/(n1::numeric/e1),2) rate_ratio, round(e2::numeric/e1,2) eff_ratio, round(c2::numeric/c1,2) cell_ratio
FROM tc JOIN eff USING (taxon_concept_id) JOIN corpus.taxa t USING (taxon_concept_id) ORDER BY rate_ratio ASC

confidence.basis: Wild records, 0.1° cells. Three continuously running sources each show fewer occupied cells despite more bird effort; looking at eBird alone removes the VBA artefact. Weaknesses: this is a nomadic species whose occurrence swings with mistletoe and rainfall, and a reporting rate built from record counts is a proxy, not occupancy.

input.summary: Painted Honeyeater is being reported less often relative to effort, and from fewer places. In eBird alone, its records per unit of bird effort fell to 0.68 of the 2017–19 level in 2022–24 and occupied cells fell from 183 to 151, while bird effort in those cells rose 1.71×. Birdata (92 to 48 cells) and BioNet (53 to 29 cells) agree. This is worth a targeted check of mistletoe-woodland sites, keeping its nomadism in mind.

confidence.basis: eBird-only records against Aves effort in the occupied cells, 2017–19 v 2022–24, with thousands of records per species. Weaknesses: record counts ignore flock size, and growing effort at non-wader sites inside coastal cells can dilute rates. Eastern Curlew and Great Knot sit near 1.0 under the same method, which suggests the method is not biased downward across the board.

input.summary: Several migratory shorebirds are reported less often relative to effort. In eBird, Curlew Sandpiper's reporting rate fell to 0.73 of its 2017–19 level, Sharp-tailed Sandpiper to 0.68, Latham's Snipe to 0.63, and Common Greenshank and Black-tailed Godwit to 0.82. Under the same method Eastern Curlew and Great Knot held steady (about 1.0). Curlew Sandpiper records stayed flat (13,534 to 13,266) while bird effort nearly doubled. These are candidates to cross-check against the Shorebirds 2020 count data.

confidence.basis: Cell counts are low and Regent Honeyeaters move with flowering, so a three-year window may catch different nectar years. Part of the cell loss is VBA (24 cells, then none). But BioNet and Birdata both run in both periods and roughly halve their cells while effort rises, so the contraction is not just a source artefact. Captive-release birds are not flagged as managed in this view, so some records may be released birds.

input.summary: Regent Honeyeater is being found at about half as many places: 126 occupied 0.1° cells in 2017–19 against 64 in 2022–24. BioNet (63 to 36) and Birdata (36 to 19) both contract. eBird records nearly tripled, but they come from fewer cells (25 to 12), which looks like birders returning to a few known sites. Rising record counts should not be read as recovery. Spatial coverage is the more telling signal, and it is shrinking.

Pacific Ridley records fell from 774 to 22 and Freshwater Sawfish from 225 to 3 (2017–19 vs 2022–24) when NESP compilations ended. Caveats: 2022–24 were mostly wet La Niña years, and birders may target newly listed or charismatic species more (Diamond Firetail was newly prominent). A rate per record of effort is not abundance.

input.summary: Some birds are holding or improving relative to effort in eBird. The 3 'wild' Central Rock-rat records in the Great Sandy Desert are probably haven animals and should be added to the managed rule.

content.text:
I've recorded 35 insights. The main finding: much of what looks like change in this data is records arriving, stopping or shifting, not species. Here is what to take from it, most important first.

## Where you are blind
- **Recent data is too thin to judge anything.** eBird holds nothing after 31 Aug 2025, and BirdLife's Birdata nothing after June 2026. Since July 2026 the record is mostly iNaturalist plus a small NSW atlas feed. Do not read any 2025–26 drop as decline.
- **Whole states and regions are effectively unmonitored for non-bird species:**
  - **Northern Territory:** the NT government's fauna atlas fell from 4,440 records in 2018 to none after March 2024, and the NESP northern research compilation ends in 2020.
  - **Queensland:** its state atlas gave only 827 threatened-species records in 2022–24.
  - **Western Australia and Tasmania:** no state atlas feeds this data at all.
  - **Arid interior:** in 2022–24 there were 2 records in the Little Sandy Desert, 6 in the Tanami and 31 in the Gibson Desert.
- **Some flagship species are missing because of how their listing is linked to records.** The koala (Qld, NSW and ACT) has 8 records in almost 12 years and the Southern Cassowary has 3. Their listings sit on population-level names that ordinary sightings never match.
- **At least 30 listed birds get nothing from eBird**, the largest dataset. Most are listed as subspecies, which eBird can't resolve to (e.g. South-eastern Brown Treecreeper, Glossy Black-cockatoo). Plains Wanderer and Orange-bellied Parrot are probably withheld as sensitive.
- **Other gaps:**
  - FrogID has delivered nothing since Nov 2024, so frog records from 2025 are not comparable with earlier years.
  - Marine turtle, sawfish and whale records collapsed when research compilations ended (e.g. Pacific Ridley turtle 774 to 22).
  - Of 392 Critically Endangered taxa, 178 have fewer than 10 records since 2015.
  - Only 46.9% of wild records are located to within 2 km.
- **Gone quiet, but probably a data gap:** four northern taxa have no records for 4–9 years: Black-footed Tree-rat (Djintamoonga), the Melville Island tree-rat, Carpentarian Rock-rat and New Guinea River Shark. All were carried only by sources that have stopped. Ask the NT government and the NESP projects for current data before concluding anything.

## What is concerning (moderate confidence: adjusted for recording effort, cross-checked between independent sources)
- **Painted Honeyeater** is reported less often relative to effort (0.68 in eBird), from fewer places (183 to 151 grid cells). Birdata independently agrees.
- **Migratory shorebirds:** Curlew Sandpiper, Sharp-tailed Sandpiper, Latham's Snipe, Common Greenshank and Black-tailed Godwit are down 0.63–0.82 in eBird, with Birdata agreeing. Eastern Curlew and Great Knot hold steady under the same method.
- **Regent Honeyeater** is now found at about half as many places (126 to 64 cells). eBird records rose, but from fewer cells, which looks like birders returning to known sites rather than recovery.
- **Weaker signals to raise with the custodians:**
  - Canberra Grassland Earless Dragon: occupied cells fell from 11–14 to 4–8.
  - Leadbeater's Possum: 18 cells in 2024 against 24–34 in earlier years.
  - Northern Quoll: AWC monitoring in WA fell to 17 records in 2024 while AWC's overall output stayed high.
- **Swift Parrot is ambiguous**: up in eBird, down in Birdata. Don't cite this data either way.

## What is new
- **Lax Leek-orchid (Critically Endangered):** the first records since 2015 arrived in late September 2026, 47 iNaturalist sightings in the Eyre Yorke Block (SA). They need expert verification now, while plants are flowering.
- **Other newly documented populations:** Elusive Bush-pea (Sydney Basin), Large-flower Groundsel (SA) and Lord Howe Placostylus snail. Several Critically Endangered taxa were also recorded in new bioregions in 2025–26 and each needs checking.
- **Fenced havens and reintroductions:** at least 27 new series have started since 2020. Since 2020 these managed records outnumber wild ones for threatened mammals (56,144 vs 16,381 in 2024), and wild Bilbies have produced at most 6 records a year. Always separate managed from wild in status work.
- **Kangaroo Island:** after the 2019–20 fires, the Kangaroo Island Dunnart is still detected across a steady 15–17 cells even as monitoring eased.

## Things that look like change but aren't
- **Golden Sun Moth's** "collapse" is one Victorian survey program ending (7,703 records in 2018 to 79 in 2021).
- **Victoria's atlas** bird records fell about tenfold after 2019, which inflates apparent declines for several Victorian birds.
- **Grey-headed Flying-fox** records fell but the area it occupies didn't.
- **Australasian Bittern's** "increase" is one Birdata survey; in eBird it is flat.
- **For 40% of well-recorded threatened plants,** most records come from a single year's survey, so plant "crashes" are mostly one-off censuses.

One error to fix in the saved records: in the Kangaroo Island post-fire insight I tagged the wrong related species. I listed the Yellow-bellied Glider subspecies (Petaurus australis brevirostrum) where it should have been Kangaroo Island Glossy Black-cockatoo, and it can't be edited from here. Two other insights (Northern Quoll, Leadbeater's Possum) were saved without a species ID attached.
